data.title: Rapamycin and human longevity among kidney transplant recipients surviving the first year.

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Human (US national organ transplant registry: 4,885 kidney transplant recipients prescribed rapamycin vs 6,589 not prescribed; alive with functioning graft at 1 year; median follow-up 11 years)
data.finding: In a US registry cohort of 11,474 kidney transplant recipients who were alive with a functioning graft at one year, 4,885 were prescribed rapamycin and 6,589 were not; 6,443 died during a median follow-up of 11 years. After propensity-score weighting for age, BMI, diabetes and 15 other factors, median survival age was 64.6 years with rapamycin and 64.3 years without (95% CI for the difference -1.6 to 2.0 years), so no meaningful survival benefit was seen. Boundary: observational registry data in transplant recipients who are also on other immunosuppressants and who entered the cohort only by having survived twelve months after transplant, rapamycin given at immunosuppressive doses by clinician choice; it does not test low-dose or intermittent rapamycin in healthy older adults.
data.abstract_excerpt: Rapamycin, an mTOR inhibitor, continues to be investigated for hypothesized physiological, disease prevention, and longevity benefits, but few studies have been conducted in humans. Using US national organ transplant registry data, one of the largest real-world datasets examining chronic rapamycin exposure in humans, we compared the Kaplan-Meier survival age distribution of 4885 kidney transplant recipients prescribed rapamycin compared to 6589 recipients not prescribed rapamycin. Recipients were followed a median of 11 years and 6443 died during the study period.
